<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">JPmHC
<br class="ltx_break">Dynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

</span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">February 2026</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in deep learning, exemplified by Hyper-Connections (HC), have expanded the residual connection paradigm by introducing wider residual streams and diverse connectivity patterns. While these innovations yield significant performance gains, they compromise the identity mapping property of residual connections, leading to training instability, limited scalability, and increased memory overhead. To address these challenges, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">JPmHC</span> (<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">J</span>acobian-spectrum <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">P</span>reserving <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">m</span>anifold-constrained <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">H</span>yper-<span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">C</span>onnections), a framework that replaces identity skips with a trainable linear mixer acting on <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> parallel streams while explicitly controlling gradient conditioning. By constraining the mixer <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> on operator-norm-bounded manifolds (e.g., bistochastic, Stiefel, Grassmann), JPmHC prevents gradient pathologies and enhances stability.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">JPmHC introduces three key contributions: (i) a free-probability analysis that predicts Jacobian spectra for structured skips, providing actionable design rules for mixer selection; (ii) memory-efficient implicit differentiation for fixed-point projections, reducing activation memory and synchronization overhead; and (iii) a Stiefel-constrained mixer via Cayley transforms, ensuring orthogonality without post-hoc normalization. Empirical evaluations on ARC-AGI demonstrate that JPmHC achieves faster convergence, higher accuracy, and lower computational cost compared to bistochastic baselines. As a flexible and scalable extension of HC, JPmHC advances spectrum-aware, stable, and efficient deep learning, offering insights into topological architecture design and foundational model evolution. 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break"></p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Disclaimer: This paper was prepared for informational purposes by the LLM Suite group of JP Morgan Chase and its affiliates (‘JPMC’) and is not a product of the Research Department of JP Morgan. <section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The residual connection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016</a>)</cite>—the per-layer update <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l+1}=F(x^{l})+x^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l+1}=F(x^{l})+x^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>—is a defining feature of modern deep learning, underpinning Transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite> and virtually every large-scale architecture deployed today. Its variants—Pre-Norm, DeepNorm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>—have enabled training at thousands of layers by smoothing loss landscapes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2018</a>)</cite> and stabilizing gradient flow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tarnowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. However, the identity skip biases layerwise mappings toward the identity, anchoring the function class and limiting expressivity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A natural generalization replaces the identity skip with a learned linear map,</p>
<table id="S1.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\text{out}}=H_{\text{res}}\,x+F(x)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mtext>out</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\text{out}}=H_{\text{res}}\,x+F(x),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">increasing expressivity but risking gradient instability if the operator norm <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|H_{\text{res}}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|H_{\text{res}}\|</annotation></semantics></math> and the singular spectrum of the end-to-end Jacobian are not controlled. To decouple expressivity from identity anchoring while preserving trainability at scale, Hyper-Connections (HC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> split the hidden state into <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> parallel streams and mix them through a small <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times n</annotation></semantics></math> matrix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Let each stream live in <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>p</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> and stack the streams so that <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{p}\cong\mathbb{R}^{np}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><mo>≅</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{p}\cong\mathbb{R}^{np}</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\ll p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\ll p</annotation></semantics></math> (typically <math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=512</annotation></semantics></math>). The HC block takes the form</p>
<table id="S1.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{\text{out}}=\bigl(H_{\text{res}}(x)\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,x+\bigl(H_{\text{post}}(x)\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,F\!\bigl(\bigl(H_{\text{pre}}(x)\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,x\bigr)," display="block" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{\text{out}}=\bigl(H_{\text{res}}(x)\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,x+\bigl(H_{\text{post}}(x)\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,F\!\bigl(\bigl(H_{\text{pre}}(x)\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,x\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\text{res}}(x),H_{\text{pre}}(x),H_{\text{post}}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>pre</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>post</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\text{res}}(x),H_{\text{pre}}(x),H_{\text{post}}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> are small mixing matrices that depend on the input <math id="S1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. The extra cost scales with <math id="S1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> and remains negligible since <math id="S1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>F</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F</annotation></semantics></math> is evaluated once per block on a stream mixture and re-distributed.
The network learns <em id="S1.p3.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">which</em> information flows where—a strictly richer connection pattern. The gains are most dramatic in the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) setting, where HC halved the training tokens needed to match baseline on OLMoE and improved BBH and GSM8K by <math id="S1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7</annotation></semantics></math> points on DeepSeek’s 27B MoE model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Both MoE and HC are learnable routing mechanisms—one for tokens across experts, the other for residual streams across layers—and both face the same stability challenge: unconstrained, they diverge (signal gains exceeding <math id="S1.p3.m11" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3000\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3000\times</annotation></semantics></math> at 27B scale <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> addressed this instability by projecting <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\text{res}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\text{res}}</annotation></semantics></math> onto the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices via the Sinkhorn–Knopp iteration. Doubly stochastic mixers are appealing because (i) their operator norm is bounded by <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>, preventing gradient explosion, and (ii) they act as transport plans <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Villani, 2003</a>)</cite>, intuitively preserving information across streams. At 27B-parameter scale, mHC demonstrated strong results with minimal overhead. However, two limitations remain: (1) operator-norm boundedness does not preclude <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">vanishing</em> gradients—a full singular-spectrum analysis of the end-to-end Jacobian is absent; and (2) backpropagating through iterative projections introduces memory and synchronization overhead in distributed training.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This is where the argument breaks down. Training deep networks requires that the singular values of the input-output Jacobian <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=\prod_{l=1}^{L}Y^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=\prod_{l=1}^{L}Y^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> remain concentrated near <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>—a property called <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">dynamical isometry</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saxe et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. Without it, expressivity capacity is lost or, worse, gradients may either explode or vanish exponentially. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tarnowski et al. (2019)</a></cite> proved that for scalar skip connections, dynamical isometry is universal: for any activation function, it is achieved when a single condition on the weight variance is met. A generalization of their free probability method to general twisting of the skip-connection seems within reach to go beyond operator-norm boundedness. For clarity-sake, we analyse the spectra for a simplified (<a href="#S1.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>):</p>
<table id="S1.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l+1}=\bigl(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,x^{l}+\phi(W^{l}x^{l}),\quad N=np," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l+1}=\bigl(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p}\bigr)\,x^{l}+\phi(W^{l}x^{l}),\quad N=np,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S1.p5.2" class="ltx_p">where each <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> is a fixed mixing matrix (independent of <math id="S1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>) for theoretical analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We extend the theory to the operator-valued setting via operator-valued free probability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Voiculescu, 1995</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dykema, 2007</a>)</cite>, where the Kronecker structure of (<a href="#S1.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) collapses the spectral problem from network width <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=np" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=np</annotation></semantics></math> to twist dimension <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>. This reveals two failure modes of doubly stochastic skip connections. The first is <em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">eigenvalue contraction</em>: a doubly stochastic matrix has its Perron eigenvalue pinned at one, but generically all others lie strictly inside the unit disk, and deep composition drives <math id="S1.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\lambda|^{L}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\lambda|^{L}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>. The second is <em id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">eigenspace misalignment</em>: eigenbases of successive layers are unrelated, so composition scrambles directions and accelerates the collapse beyond what per-layer spectra predict. Together, these produce a partial spectral collapse—a growing fraction of the Jacobian’s singular values drifting toward zero—that no reparametrisation of the Birkhoff polytope can escape.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Orthogonal matrices eliminate both failure modes: all eigenvalues lie on the unit circle, so no contraction is possible, and group closure under composition prevents misalignment at any depth. We propose replacing the Birkhoff constraint with the orthogonal group <math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n)</annotation></semantics></math>, parametrised via the Cayley transform <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lezcano-Casado, 2019</a>)</cite>, which maps skew-symmetric matrices to orthogonal ones via <math id="S1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(I-S)(I+S)^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Beyond spectral preservation, this provides a strictly richer function class (the linear span of <math id="S1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n)</annotation></semantics></math> is the full algebra <math id="S1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{n}(\mathbb{R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{n}(\mathbb{R})</annotation></semantics></math>, dimension <math id="S1.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, versus <math id="S1.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(n{-}1)^{2}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(n{-}1)^{2}+1</annotation></semantics></math> for the Birkhoff polytope) and implicit geometric nonlinearity from the curvature of the orthogonal manifold.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span></p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spectral diagnosis.</span> We identify eigenvalue contraction and eigenspace misalignment as the mechanisms by which doubly stochastic skip connections break dynamical isometry, and show that this collapse converts to concrete capacity loss in modern training (<em id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">spectral stalling</em>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cayley-transform Stiefel projection.</span> We instantiate an orthogonality-preserving mixer by projecting <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{\text{res}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>res</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{\text{res}}</annotation></semantics></math> onto the Stiefel manifold via a small, fixed number of Cayley iterations (as few as <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=2</annotation></semantics></math>), yielding norm-preserving mixing with exact gradients and negligible overhead <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lezcano-Casado, 2019</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Grassmannian subspace mixer.</span> We develop a rank-<math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> variant with <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(np)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(np)</annotation></semantics></math> parameters that mixes through a learned <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspace, optimized with a Cayley retraction for efficient Riemannian updates.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implicit differentiation for fixed-point projections.</span> We design a custom backward pass for iterative normalizations and projections (e.g., Sinkhorn for bistochastic constraints, Cayley for orthogonal constraints), reducing activation memory from <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(T)</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(1)</annotation></semantics></math> and eliminating distributed data-parallel synchronization stalls, while remaining compatible with CUDA graphs and mixed precision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eisenberger et al., 2022a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">5.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Operator-valued Dyson pipeline.</span> We develop the first numerical implementation of the full operator-valued free probability pipeline—from the matrix Dyson equation through Dykema’s twisted S-transform multiplicativity to multi-layer spectral densities.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">6.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental validation.</span> We confirm the spectral predictions against Monte Carlo simulation and validate the practical consequence on a modified Tiny Recursive Model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025</a>)</cite> evaluated on ARC-AGI-1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chollet, 2019</a>)</cite>: orthogonal skip connections converge faster and reach higher accuracy than bistochastic ones.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Spectral Analysis</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now develop the spectral machinery for predicting the singular-value distribution of the end-to-end Jacobian in deep networks with structured skip connections. The key insight is that free probability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Voiculescu, 1991</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nica and Speicher, 2006</a>)</cite> reduces the spectral analysis of <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-layer compositions to fixed-point equations on order parameters, and the Kronecker structure <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}\otimes I_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}\otimes I_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> further collapses the problem from network width <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=np" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=np</annotation></semantics></math> to twist dimension <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Scalar Dyson equation and dynamical isometry</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Consider a standard residual network with scalar skip connection <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and layer-wise update <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{l+1}=\phi(W^{l}x^{l})+ax^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{l+1}=\phi(W^{l}x^{l})+ax^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. The linearized layer map is <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{l}=D^{l}W^{l}+aI_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{l}=D^{l}W^{l}+aI_{N}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{l}=\mathrm{diag}(\phi^{\prime}(h^{l}_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>diag</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{l}=\mathrm{diag}(\phi^{\prime}(h^{l}_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}</annotation></semantics></math> has i.i.d. Gaussian entries with variance <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{w}^{2}/N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{w}^{2}/N</annotation></semantics></math>. The end-to-end Jacobian is <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J=\prod_{l=1}^{L}Y^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J=\prod_{l=1}^{L}Y^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In the mean-field limit (<math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>), the activation derivatives <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> concentrate around their expectation, making <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{l}W^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{l}W^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> effectively isotropic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. Free probability theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Voiculescu, 1991</a>)</cite> then predicts the limiting spectral density of <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{\top}J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{\top}J</annotation></semantics></math> via the <em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Cauchy transform</em> <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G(z):=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\mathrm{Tr}(zI-J^{\top}J)^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">:=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Tr</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G(z):=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\mathrm{Tr}(zI-J^{\top}J)^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and the <em id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">S-transform</em>, which linearizes free multiplicative convolution: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="S_{J^{\top}J}(w)=\prod_{l=1}^{L}S_{Y^{l}{}^{\top}Y^{l}}(w)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><msubsup><mo>∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>Y</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>l</mi></msup><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mi>Y</mi><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{J^{\top}J}(w)=\prod_{l=1}^{L}S_{Y^{l}{}^{\top}Y^{l}}(w)</annotation></semantics></math>. One can deduce <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> and vice-versa,</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For scalar skip connections, Tarnowski et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tarnowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite> derived a scalar fixed-point equation for the single-layer Cauchy transform. The order parameter <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(z)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies the <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">scalar Dyson equation</em>:</p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(z)=\frac{a}{z-\sigma^{2}m(z)},\quad\text{where}\quad\sigma^{2}=\sigma_{w}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\phi^{\prime}(\sqrt{q}Z)^{2}]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mtext>where</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝔼</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msqrt><mi>q</mi></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(z)=\frac{a}{z-\sigma^{2}m(z)},\quad\text{where}\quad\sigma^{2}=\sigma_{w}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\phi^{\prime}(\sqrt{q}Z)^{2}],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> is the forward signal variance, <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>. The Cauchy transform is <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{Y^{\top}Y}(z)=m(z)/z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{Y^{\top}Y}(z)=m(z)/z</annotation></semantics></math>. For <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> identical layers, the <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>-mapping converts <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{Y^{\top}Y}(w)^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{Y^{\top}Y}(w)^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> back to <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G_{J^{\top}J}(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G_{J^{\top}J}(z)</annotation></semantics></math> without numerically fragile S-transform inversion.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A network achieves <em id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">dynamical isometry</em> when the singular values of its Jacobian <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> concentrate near <math id="S2.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>. For scalar skip connections, regardless of activation function or depth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tarnowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, dynamical isometry is achieved via suitable scaling of layers weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This universality breaks down for structured skip connections: when <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> is replaced by an <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times n</annotation></semantics></math> matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, the scalar trace <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Tr</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}</annotation></semantics></math> averages over <math id="S2.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>’s spectral sectors. Scalar approximation distinguishes bistochastic and orthogonal mixer but predictions are inaccurate for bistochastic (mHC) and general linear (HC) mixers, see figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Operator-valued multi-layer pipeline. ‣ 2.3 Numerical pipeline ‣ 2 Spectral Analysis ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Operator-valued extension: Kronecker collapse</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hyper-Connections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> replace the scalar skip with a Kronecker product <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=A_{n}\otimes I_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=A_{n}\otimes I_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> mixes <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> parallel streams of dimension <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=np" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=np</annotation></semantics></math>. The layer-wise Jacobian becomes</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{l}=(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p})+D^{l}W^{l}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{l}=(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p})+D^{l}W^{l},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}</annotation></semantics></math> remains isotropic Gaussian, but the skip structure is now block-diagonal with <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times n</annotation></semantics></math> blocks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why scalar theory fails.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The scalar Cauchy transform <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G(z)=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}(zI_{N}-M)^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Tr</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G(z)=\frac{1}{N}\mathrm{Tr}(zI_{N}-M)^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> computes an average over all <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> eigenvalues. When <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=(A_{n}\otimes I_{p})+\text{noise}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mtext>noise</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=(A_{n}\otimes I_{p})+\text{noise}</annotation></semantics></math>, this trace averages over the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> spectral sectors induced by <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, collapsing eigenvalue structure that is critical for gradient flow. For instance, if <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is bistochastic with eigenvalues <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\lambda_{i}|&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\lambda_{i}|&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\geq 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\geq 2</annotation></semantics></math>, the scalar theory sees only the average behavior, not the sector-wise contraction that drives vanishing gradients.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Operator-valued free probability.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The solution is to work over the base algebra <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}=M_{n}(\mathbb{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}=M_{n}(\mathbb{C})</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Voiculescu, 1995</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Speicher, 1998</a>)</cite>. We promote the order parameter from a scalar <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m(z)\in\mathbb{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℂ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m(z)\in\mathbb{C}</annotation></semantics></math> to a matrix <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(z)\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(z)\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})</annotation></semantics></math>, and the Cauchy transform to a <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math>-valued functional. The Kronecker structure <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}\otimes I_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}\otimes I_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> ensures that the self-consistent equation for <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(z)</annotation></semantics></math> depends only on <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and the noise variance <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, not on the stream dimension <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Critically, the S-transform multiplicativity rule becomes <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">twisted</em> in the operator-valued setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dykema, 2007</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{XY}(B)=S_{Y}(B)\,S_{X}\bigl(S_{Y}(B)^{-1}BS_{Y}(B)\bigr),\quad B\in\mathcal{B}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Y</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{XY}(B)=S_{Y}(B)\,S_{X}\bigl(S_{Y}(B)^{-1}BS_{Y}(B)\bigr),\quad B\in\mathcal{B}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">This conjugation by <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{Y}(B)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>B</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{Y}(B)</annotation></semantics></math> encodes the eigenspace rotation between successive layers when <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{n}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{n}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> do not commute—precisely the misalignment effect absent in scalar theory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Kronecker collapse)<span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Under the Kronecker structure <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y^{l}=(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p})+D^{l}W^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>Y</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y^{l}=(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p})+D^{l}W^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and mean-field isotropy, the <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math>-valued order parameter <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(z)\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(z)\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})</annotation></semantics></math> defined for <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies the matrix fixed-point equation</span></p>
<table id="S2.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(z)=A_{h}(M)\cdot\bigl(zI_{n}-A_{h}(z)^{\top}A_{h}(z)\bigr)^{-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(z)=A_{h}(M)\cdot\bigl(zI_{n}-A_{h}(z)^{\top}A_{h}(z)\bigr)^{-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{h}(z):=A_{n}+\sigma^{2}z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{h}(z):=A_{n}+\sigma^{2}z</annotation></semantics></math> is the <em id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">dressed matrix</em>. The scalar Cauchy transform is recovered by <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G(z)=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{Tr}_{n}\bigl(zI_{n}-A_{h}(z)^{\top}A_{h}(z)\bigr)^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>Tr</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G(z)=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{Tr}_{n}\bigl(zI_{n}-A_{h}(z)^{\top}A_{h}(z)\bigr)^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. When <math id="S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=1</annotation></semantics></math>, this reduces to (<a href="#S2.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 2.1 Scalar Dyson equation and dynamical isometry ‣ 2 Spectral Analysis ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proof sketch.</span> The key steps are: (i) the Kronecker structure implies <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}[W^{l}(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p})]=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>W</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}[W^{l}(A_{n}^{l}\otimes I_{p})]=0</annotation></semantics></math> by isotropy; (ii) the self-energy <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma(z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma(z)</annotation></semantics></math> has the block form <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{n}\otimes I_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{n}\otimes I_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma_{n}\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ℂ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma_{n}\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C})</annotation></semantics></math>; (iii) inserting the ansatz <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(z)=M_{n}(z)\otimes I_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(z)=M_{n}(z)\otimes I_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> into the Dyson-Schwinger equation and tracing over the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p\times p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p\times p</annotation></semantics></math> blocks yields (<a href="#S2.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Proposition 2.1 (Kronecker collapse). ‣ Operator-valued free probability. ‣ 2.2 Operator-valued extension: Kronecker collapse ‣ 2 Spectral Analysis ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computational complexity.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Solving (<a href="#S2.E7" title="Equation 7 ‣ Proposition 2.1 (Kronecker collapse). ‣ Operator-valued free probability. ‣ 2.2 Operator-valued extension: Kronecker collapse ‣ 2 Spectral Analysis ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>) requires Newton iteration in <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> at cost <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n^{6})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>6</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n^{6})</annotation></semantics></math> per step (matrix inversion dominates). Since <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\ll p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\ll p</annotation></semantics></math> (typically <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=4</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=512" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>512</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=512</annotation></semantics></math>), this collapses the spectral problem from <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(N^{3})=O((np)^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(N^{3})=O((np)^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n^{6})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>6</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n^{6})</annotation></semantics></math>, a reduction of factor <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(p/n)^{3}\approx 10^{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>≈</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(p/n)^{3}\approx 10^{5}</annotation></semantics></math> at typical scales. This makes exhaustive spectral analysis tractable for networks of arbitrary width <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Numerical pipeline</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now describe the computational methods for solving the scalar and operator-valued Dyson equations and extracting spectral densities.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scalar solver.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For fixed <math id="S2.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℂ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> (upper half-plane), equation (<a href="#S2.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 2.1 Scalar Dyson equation and dynamical isometry ‣ 2 Spectral Analysis ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) is solved by Newton’s method with the iteration</p>
<table id="S2.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
