<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyper-Connections and structured skip connections</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the references on which our work is buit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, two concurrent works explore related directions: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang and Gao (2026)</a></cite> parametrises doubly stochastic matrices as Kronecker products of smaller bistochastic factors via the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alonso (2026)</a></cite> proposes an operator-constrained framework. All of these remain within the Birkhoff polytope. Our work departs from this line by showing that the polytope’s contractive geometry causes spectral collapse, and proposes the orthogonal group as the correct constraint manifold.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimization on Matrix Manifolds.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Optimization over structured matrix sets has a rich history. The Cayley transform for parameterizing orthogonal matrices dates to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cayley (1846)</a></cite>, with modern applications in neural networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020b</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Absil et al. (2008)</a></cite> provides principled gradient descent on curved spaces. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ablin et al. (2024)</a></cite> study the soft landing approach. The Sinkhorn operator and its differentiable variants have been extensively studied for optimal transport <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinkhorn, 1967</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Eisenberger et al., 2022b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Orthogonal constraints in neural networks</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Orthogonal and unitary weight constraints have a rich history in recurrent networks, where they prevent gradient decay across time steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arjovsky et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wisdom et al., 2016</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lezcano-Casado (2019)</a></cite> developed a general framework for gradient-based optimisation on matrix manifolds via trivializations (exponential map, Cayley transform), enabling efficient training with hard orthogonal constraints. We apply these parametrisation techniques not to weight matrices but to the skip connection matrices <math id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> in Hyper-Connections, motivated by our spectral analysis showing that orthogonality of <math id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{q}</annotation></semantics></math> is the decisive property for preserving dynamical isometry.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Signal propagation and mean-field theory</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The mean-field theory of deep networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schoenholz et al. (2017)</a></cite> studies the propagation of pre-activation moments, identifying the edge-of-chaos phase transition. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang and Schoenholz (2017)</a></cite> extended this to residual networks. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pennington et al. (2017)</a></cite> connected signal propagation to the Jacobian’s singular value distribution, introducing dynamical isometry for nonlinear networks. These works characterise signal propagation through scalar order parameters; our work computes the full spectral density, revealing failure modes—such as partial spectral collapse in bistochastic skip connections—that are invisible to mean-field analysis. To the best of our knowledge, operator valued free probability calculus for Neural Networks Jabobian spectrum comnputation has been introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang (2020)</a></cite>. In particular, Operator-valued freeness is proved there.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Recursive Reasoning Models.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025)</a></cite> introduced recursive multi-step reasoning with deep supervision for puzzle-solving tasks. The Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jolicoeur-Martineau (2025)</a></cite> simplified HRM to a single 2-layer network with weight-tied recursion, achieving state-of-the-art results on ARC-AGI-1 (45% accuracy) with only 7M parameters. We adopt the TRM architecture as our evaluation platform, extending it with structured multi-stream mixing.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="S7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.1 </span>Why Does Cayley Outperform Sinkhorn?</h3>

<div id="S7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results show a consistent advantage for the Cayley JPmHC variant over implicit Sinkhorn, with the gap most pronounced in exact-match accuracy (<math id="S7.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.41\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.41</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.41\times</annotation></semantics></math>). We hypothesize several contributing factors:</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bistochastic Induces Spectral Stalling</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Spectral Stalling is the phenomenon by which directions associated with small singular values are ignored during the gradient descent: there is a hard cutoff of the spectrum. Effectively, the spectrum acts as a filter on the parameter space, the model is trained only on the subspace associated with singular values above the threshold.
As shown in <a href="#S2" title="2 Spectral Analysis ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, Orthogonal and Bistochastic skip-connections show substantial differences in Jacobian singular spectrum. On the one hand, orthogonal skip-connection is undistinguishable from identity skip-connection, therefore dynamical isometry is achieved, the whole spectrum is above threshold. On the other hand, bistochastic skip-connection shows that more than 75% of the spectral mass is concentrated around 0, which suggest the same fraction of the weights are ignored: the model capacity is reduced.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Orthogonal Has Full Mixing Expressivity</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The respective intrinsic dimension of Orthogonal matrices and Bistochastic matrices are <math id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(q-1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(q-1)/2</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{2}-2q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{2}-2q</annotation></semantics></math> suggesting that Bistochastic matrices are more expressive. However, the latter form a polytope (a linear object) while the former form a spherical domain (non-linear). The span of Orthogonal matrices is the whole space of mixing matrices with dimension <math id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> while the span of Bistochastic matrices has dimension <math id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q^{2}-2q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q^{2}-2q</annotation></semantics></math>. The non-linear structure of orthogonal matrices has full mixing expressivity, while bistochastic matrices do not.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Computational Efficiency.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Cayley JPmHC variant requires <math id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\sim}2.25\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>2.25</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}2.25\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer FLOPs per module (<a href="#S5.T5" title="In 5.2 Compute-Accuracy Tradeoff ‣ 5 Results ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), enabling more optimization steps per unit of wall-clock time.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.2 </span>Implicit Differentiation: Correctness and Efficiency</h3>

<div id="S7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The custom backward pass for Sinkhorn (<a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Sinkhorn Variant with Implicit Differentiation ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>) achieves two goals simultaneously:</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S7.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S7.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memory reduction</span>: From <math id="S7.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(T)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(T)</annotation></semantics></math> intermediate tensors to <math id="S7.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(1)</annotation></semantics></math> (only the output <math id="S7.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DDP compatibility</span>: Elimination of 128K autograd nodes that caused synchronization stalls in distributed training.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The key insight is that Sinkhorn’s fixed-point structure admits a closed-form implicit derivative. The Jacobian-vector product of the Sinkhorn operator at its fixed point can be expressed as a linear system involving only the fixed point <math id="S7.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}</annotation></semantics></math> itself, bypassing the need to unroll through <math id="S7.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> iterations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Self-Stabilization.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An important property of the implicit gradient formula (<a href="#A8.E23" title="Equation 23 ‣ Proposition H.1 (Implicit Sinkhorn Gradient [ ] ). ‣ Backward Pass. ‣ H.2 Solution: Custom Autograd Function with Implicit Differentiation ‣ Appendix H Sinkhorn Variant with Implicit Differentiation ‣ JPmHCDynamical Isometry via Orthogonal Hyper-Connections" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a>) is <em id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">self-stabilization</em>: the Hadamard product <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\odot(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\odot(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> automatically zeros out gradient contributions to entries where <math id="S7.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{ij}\approx 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{ij}\approx 0</annotation></semantics></math>, preventing gradient flow through near-zero mixing weights. This is analogous to the “straight-through” behavior of hard attention, but arises naturally from the fixed-point structure.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.3 </span>Comparison with Hyper-Connections and mHC</h3>

<div id="S7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our JPmHC framework extends both the original HC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and the concurrent mHC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> in several dimensions:</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S7.T6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S7.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Feature comparison with HC and mHC.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S7.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.4 </span>Limitations</h3>

<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Unmatched Training Budgets.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The most significant limitation is that the Cayley and Sinkhorn variants have been trained for different numbers of steps (419K vs. 349K). Although Sinkhorn has significantly closed the gap since earlier checkpoints, the performance ratio has stabilized around <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.19\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.19</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.19\times</annotation></semantics></math> for pass@1 and <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.41\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.41</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.41\times</annotation></semantics></math> for exact-match, suggesting a genuine asymptotic advantage for Cayley. Final conclusions still require matched-compute comparisons.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pre/Post Architecture Confound.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As noted, the Cayley and Sinkhorn variants differ in pre/post normalization and mapping architecture, making it impossible to attribute the entire performance gap to the manifold choice alone.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Single Architecture.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments use the 7M-parameter TRM on ARC-AGI. Generalization to larger models, different architectures, and other tasks (language modeling, vision) remains to be validated.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Incomplete Variant Coverage.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Grassmann, variant have been implemented and unit-tested but not yet trained at scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Small <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=4</annotation></semantics></math> streams, the permutation group <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{4}</annotation></semantics></math> has only 24 elements, making exhaustive spectral gap analysis tractable. For <math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\geq 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\geq 7</annotation></semantics></math> (<math id="S7.SS4.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n!=5040" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>5040</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n!=5040</annotation></semantics></math>), approximate methods would be needed.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented JPmHC, a unified framework of five manifold-constrained mixing strategies for multi-stream residual architectures, extending the mHC framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> with novel projection methods and efficient differentiation. Our two primary contributions—<span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">implicit Sinkhorn differentiation</span> and <span id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cayley transform projection</span>—address complementary challenges: the former eliminates DDP synchronization stalls in the Sinkhorn backward pass, while the latter provides norm-preserving orthogonal mixing with exact gradients.</p>
</div>
<section id="S8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">8.1 </span>Summary of Key Results</h3>

<div id="S8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On ARC-AGI with a 7M-parameter TRM:</p>
<ul id="S8.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S8.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Cayley JPmHC variant achieves 40.5% pass@1 and 31.4% exact-match accuracy at 419K steps—a <math id="S8.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.41\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.41</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.41\times</annotation></semantics></math> improvement in exact-match over the Sinkhorn variant.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Cayley variant reaches a 21% lower evaluation LM loss (<math id="S8.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.643" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.643</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.643</annotation></semantics></math> vs. <math id="S8.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.819" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.819</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.819</annotation></semantics></math>) and surpasses Sinkhorn’s current exact-match accuracy (22.2%) at less than half of Sinkhorn’s training budget, demonstrating superior sample efficiency.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Cayley JPmHC module requires <math id="S8.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.25\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.25</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.25\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer FLOPs than Sinkhorn while achieving higher accuracy—a Pareto improvement in both compute and quality.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The implicit-Sinkhorn variant reaches 34.1% pass@1 and 22.2% exact-match at 349K steps, with a stabilizing gap, confirming both manifold constraints are viable but Cayley maintains a persistent advantage.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both JPmHC variants exceed 85% per-token accuracy, confirming the viability of structured mixing for recursive reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S8.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Three additional JPmHC variants—Grassmannian subspace projection, spectral-gap-optimal permutations, and permutation convex hull—have been implemented, unit-tested, and integrated into our training infrastructure. Scale training of these variants is in progress and will complete the empirical picture across all five manifold constraints.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">8.2 </span>Broader Impact</h3>

<div id="S8.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work demonstrates that <em id="S8.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">geometric structure</em>—manifold constraints, group-theoretic analysis, implicit differentiation—can be profitably applied to architectural components typically treated as unconstrained parameters. By restricting mixing matrices to well-understood mathematical objects (orthogonal matrices, doubly-stochastic matrices, Grassmannians), we obtain models that are more computationally efficient and more effective. This approach is orthogonal to advances in attention mechanisms, normalization, and activation functions, suggesting potential for broader adoption in multi-stream architectures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S8.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">8.3 </span>Future Work</h3>

<div id="S8.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S8.I2" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S8.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Matched-compute comparison</span>: Complete training runs with equal compute budgets to fairly assess Cayley vs. Sinkhorn asymptotic performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pre/post ablation</span>: Isolate the contribution of manifold choice from pre/post architecture differences.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Train remaining variants</span>: Grassmann, Spectral-Gap, and Permutation Convex Hull at scale.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scale experiments</span>: Larger models (<math id="S8.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\geq 8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\geq 8</annotation></semantics></math> streams, <math id="S8.I2.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\geq 1024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\geq 1024</annotation></semantics></math>) and additional benchmarks (language modeling, ARC-AGI-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chollet et al., 2025</a>)</cite>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S8.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S8.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S8.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adaptive variant selection</span>: Learn which mixing strategy to apply at each layer during training.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_title">Deep residual learning for image recognition</span>.
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock">In <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_inbook">Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)</span>,
</span>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Matrices Manifolds</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Doubly-Stochastic Matrices and the Birkhoff Polytope</h3>

<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition A.1</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Doubly-Stochastic Matrix)<span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">A matrix <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math> is <em id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">doubly stochastic</em> if <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{ij}\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{ij}\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i,j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i,j</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏𝟏</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>𝟏</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The set of all <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times n</annotation></semantics></math> doubly-stochastic matrices forms the <em id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Birkhoff polytope</em> <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>. By the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem, <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the convex hull of the <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n!" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n!</annotation></semantics></math> permutation matrices:</p>
<table id="A1.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{n}=\mathrm{conv}\{\mathbf{P}_{\sigma}:\sigma\in S_{n}\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>conv</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{n}=\mathrm{conv}\{\mathbf{P}_{\sigma}:\sigma\in S_{n}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="(\mathbf{P}_{\sigma})_{ij}=\mathbbm{1}[\sigma(j)=i]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>σ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟙</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{P}_{\sigma})_{ij}=\mathbbm{1}[\sigma(j)=i]</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Sinkhorn-Knopp Algorithm</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinkhorn [1967]</a></cite> projects an arbitrary non-negative matrix onto the Birkhoff polytope via alternating row and column normalization. In log-space (for numerical stability):</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Sinkhorn-Knopp Projection (Log-Space)</figcaption>

<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">

            Unconstrained logit matrix <math id="alg1.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math>, iterations <math id="alg1.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">2:</span></span>
              
              
            Doubly-stochastic matrix <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\in\mathcal{B}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
              
              
            <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\mathbf{M}\leftarrow\mathrm{clamp}(\mathbf{X},-10,10)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>clamp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\mathbf{M}\leftarrow\mathrm{clamp}(\mathbf{X},-10,10)</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
              
              
            <span id="alg1.l4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1,\ldots,T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1,\ldots,T</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l4.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>
              
              
              <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\mathbf{M}\leftarrow\log\mathbf{M}-\mathrm{LSE}_{\text{row}}(\log\mathbf{M})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>LSE</mi><mtext>row</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\mathbf{M}\leftarrow\log\mathbf{M}-\mathrm{LSE}_{\text{row}}(\log\mathbf{M})</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l5.3" class="ltx_text" style="float:right;"><math id="alg1.l5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math> Row normalize
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
              
              
              <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\mathbf{M}\leftarrow\log\mathbf{M}-\mathrm{LSE}_{\text{col}}(\log\mathbf{M})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>LSE</mi><mtext>col</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\mathbf{M}\leftarrow\log\mathbf{M}-\mathrm{LSE}_{\text{col}}(\log\mathbf{M})</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l6.3" class="ltx_text" style="float:right;"><math id="alg1.l6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math> Column normalize
</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">7:</span></span>
              
              
            <span id="alg1.l7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l7.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">8:</span></span>
              
              
            <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\leftarrow\exp(\log\mathbf{M})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\leftarrow\exp(\log\mathbf{M})</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">9:</span></span>
              
              
            <span id="alg1.l9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">return</span> <math id="alg1.l9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{LSE}_{\text{row}}(\mathbf{A})_{ij}=\log\sum_{k}\exp(A_{ik})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>LSE</mi><mtext>row</mtext></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐀</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>log</mi><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>k</mi></msub><mi>exp</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{LSE}_{\text{row}}(\mathbf{A})_{ij}=\log\sum_{k}\exp(A_{ik})</annotation></semantics></math> broadcasts along rows.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>The Stiefel Manifold</h3>

<div id="A1.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition A.2</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Stiefel Manifold)<span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The Stiefel manifold <math id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(n,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(n,p)</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of <math id="A1.Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times p</annotation></semantics></math> matrices with orthonormal columns:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(n,p)=\{\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}:\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}_{p}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐔</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐈</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(n,p)=\{\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}:\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{I}_{p}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=n</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(n,n)=O(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(n,n)=O(n)</annotation></semantics></math> is the orthogonal group. Points on <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{St}(n,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{St}(n,p)</annotation></semantics></math> can be parametrized via the Cayley transform of skew-symmetric matrices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>The Grassmann Manifold</h3>

<div id="A1.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition A.3</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Grassmann Manifold)<span id="A1.Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The Grassmann manifold <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(n,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(n,p)</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional subspaces of <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(n,p)=\mathrm{St}(n,p)/O(p)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(n,p)=\mathrm{St}(n,p)/O(p),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">where <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(p)</annotation></semantics></math> acts by right multiplication. Two matrices <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathrm{St}(n,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐕</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>St</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathrm{St}(n,p)</annotation></semantics></math> represent the same point on <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Gr}(n,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Gr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Gr}(n,p)</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐕</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐔𝐐</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> for some <math id="A1.Thmtheorem3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{Q}\in O(p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐐</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{Q}\in O(p)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The canonical representation of a Grassmannian point is the orthogonal projector <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐔𝐔</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is invariant to the <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(p)</annotation></semantics></math> fiber action.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.5 </span>Cayley Transform</h3>

<div id="A1.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Cayley transform maps skew-symmetric matrices to orthogonal matrices:</p>
<table id="A1.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbf{W})=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{W}/2)(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{W}/2)^{-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Cay</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐖</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbf{W})=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{W}/2)(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{W}/2)^{-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS5.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}=-\mathbf{W}^{\top}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}=-\mathbf{W}^{\top}</annotation></semantics></math> is skew-symmetric. This mapping is a diffeomorphism from the space of skew-symmetric matrices to the connected component of <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n)</annotation></semantics></math> containing the identity (i.e., <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\det=+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">det</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\det=+1</annotation></semantics></math>), minus the set where <math id="A1.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{W}/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐈</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{W}/2</annotation></semantics></math> is singular.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Detailed Algorithm Pseudocode</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Complete Sinkhorn Implicit Backward</h3>

<figure id="alg2" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 2</span> </span> Complete Sinkhorn Implicit Backward Pass</figcaption>
<div id="alg2.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg2.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1:</span></span>
              
              
            Saved output <math id="alg2.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times n\times n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times n\times n}</annotation></semantics></math>, upstream gradient <math id="alg2.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{P}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>𝐏</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{P}}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg2.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">2:</span></span>
              
              
            Number of Gauss-Seidel iterations <math id="alg2.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> (default: <math id="alg2.l2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4n=16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4n=16</annotation></semantics></math>)

</div>
<div id="alg2.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg2.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
              
              
            Gradient <math id="alg2.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{M}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>𝐌</mi></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{M}}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>

<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Complexity Analysis</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> streams and <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> generators:</p>
<ul id="A3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Number of candidate subsets: <math id="A3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\binom{n!}{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\binom{n!}{K}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">BFS closure check: <math id="A3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(n!\cdot K)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo rspace="0.055em">!</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(n!\cdot K)</annotation></semantics></math> per subset</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Eigendecomposition: <math id="A3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}((n!)^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}((n!)^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> per valid generating set</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Total: <math id="A3.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}\!\left(\binom{n!}{K}\cdot(n!)^{3}\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.654em;" width="0.654em"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></mfrac><mo rspace="0.055em">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}\!\left(\binom{n!}{K}\cdot(n!)^{3}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

<td id="A4.T8.5.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb"><math id="A4.T8.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=6</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb"><math id="A4.T8.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(n+n+6)\times nd+22=28{,}694" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>22</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>28,694</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(n+n+6)\times nd+22=28{,}694</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="A4.T8.5.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb">+ perm indices</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With 4 unique JPmHC modules per model (2 per unique layer, weight-tied across 6 recursive cycles), the total JPmHC parameter overhead ranges from <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}115" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>115</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}115</annotation></semantics></math>K (Perm Mix) to <math id="A4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}410" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>410</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}410</annotation></semantics></math>K (Cayley), which is <math id="A4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.6</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="A4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.8\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5.8</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.8\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the <math id="A4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}7</annotation></semantics></math>M total model parameters.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Convergence of Gauss-Seidel Solver</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The convergence rate of the Gauss-Seidel solver for the implicit Sinkhorn backward depends on the spectral radius <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> of the iteration matrix. For a doubly-stochastic matrix <math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}</annotation></semantics></math> with entries bounded away from 0 and 1, the spectral radius satisfies <math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, ensuring convergence.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A5.T9.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 9</span>: </span><span id="A5.T9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Gauss-Seidel convergence for <math id="A5.T9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=4</annotation></semantics></math> with typical <math id="A5.T9.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐏</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}</annotation></semantics></math> matrices.</span></figcaption>
